opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really exciting time, even though the resource gap is real and I don't want to pretend it isn't. Frontier labs can train models at a scale that no university can match, and if academia tries to compete head-on on that axis, we'll lose. But I don't think that's where the most interesting opportunities are for us.

If you look back at the history of ML systems, a lot of the foundational ideas came from small groups asking slightly unusual questions. When we started working on XGBoost, or later on TVM and the compiler stack, we weren't the biggest team. What we had was the freedom to think about abstractions — how do you make something general, reusable, and open, so many people can build on it? That kind of work often doesn't fit neatly into the roadmap of a company that has to ship a specific model by a specific date.

So the first opportunity I see is around open infrastructure and abstractions. Things like ML compilation, efficient serving engines, structured generation — projects like MLC LLM or XGrammar — are about making models run well everywhere, on phones, browsers, different GPUs, not just the one cluster a lab happens to own. Universities are uniquely positioned to build that kind of universal, community-driven layer, because our incentive is for the ideas to be broadly adopted.

The second opportunity is that the frontier is not only about training. As models get deployed, there's a huge set of problems in inference efficiency, agentic workloads, how you co-design the system with the model, how you bring things to the edge. Many of those problems can be studied with modest compute, and the impact can be enormous, because every improvement multiplies across everyone using the models.

Third, I think the open-source ecosystem has really changed the equation. With strong open-weight models available, a university group can now experiment on top of very capable models without pretraining them. That lowers the barrier a lot, and it means we can contribute to the full stack in meaningful ways.

And finally, there's the role of training people. Students who build real systems end to end, who understand the hardware, the compiler, the model, and the application together — that's incredibly valuable, both for academia and industry. Collaboration also goes both ways; a lot of what we do happens with industry partners, and I see that as healthy rather than a competition.

So my advice to students is: don't measure yourself by how many GPUs you have. Look for the problems where a good abstraction or a clever systems idea can make everyone's resources go further. That's where academic ML systems research can have outsized impact.

r001.rationale: The response treats the resource gap as a reason for universities to pursue clever systems ideas and abstractions that make limited resources go further.

r002.rationale: It mentions academic freedom to explore abstractions, but does not identify universities as providing space for sustained research.

r003.rationale: It advocates open, community-driven infrastructure and says universities can create work that many people build on.

r004.rationale: It discusses systems components and the full stack, but does not present excelling at one critical subsystem as an alternative to building an entire AI system.

r005.rationale: It does not state that leading LLM inference kernel optimization is possible with a single current-generation GPU.

r006.rationale: It does not comment on how well-funded industrial R&D is compared with outsiders’ expectations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually one of the questions I get asked most often by students, and my honest answer is that the gap is real, but it's much less limiting than people assume, as long as you pick the right problems.

Let me start with the obvious part. If your research question is "what happens when you train a model with ten times more compute," then yes, you are going to lose that race to a frontier lab. They have the GPUs, the data, and the engineering teams, and it makes no sense to compete on that axis. But I'd argue that was never where most of the interesting ML systems work came from in the first place.

If you look at the history, a lot of the foundational ideas came out of universities working with very modest resources. When we built XGBoost, that was a grad student project on a laptop and a small cluster. TVM started with a couple of us trying to get models to run on devices that were not GPUs at all. The constraint actually shaped the research. When you cannot throw hardware at a problem, you are forced to think about the structure of the problem, and that is exactly where systems insight lives.

So the way I frame it to my students is this. Frontier labs are optimizing a fairly narrow operating point: enormous models, enormous clusters, one or two hardware vendors. That leaves a huge surface area uncovered. How do you serve these models efficiently on a single consumer GPU, or on a phone? How do you make compilers that generalize across the increasingly diverse hardware landscape? How do you do quantization, sparsity, speculative decoding, memory management for long context? These are problems where a clever idea and a good implementation beat raw scale, and where a small team can genuinely move the field. A lot of what happened with MLC LLM came out of that mindset, asking what it takes to make universal deployment possible rather than what it takes to train the biggest thing.

The second point is that open source changes the economics completely. Academia used to be disadvantaged because you could not even get your hands on a strong model. Now the open-weight ecosystem means a university group can study, optimize, and build systems around models that are quite close to the frontier. The systems layer, the compilers, the serving infrastructure, the runtime, is where a lot of the open ecosystem actually gets built, and universities are natural contributors there because we care about generality and about publishing how things work, not just that they work.

The third thing I'd say is about time horizons. Labs are under enormous pressure to ship. Universities can afford to work on something that might only matter in three to five years, like new abstractions for programming accelerators, or rethinking how we co-design hardware and software. Some of that will not pan out, and that's fine. That tolerance for longer bets is genuinely a competitive advantage, not a consolation prize.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. You do need some compute, and the field should keep pushing for shared infrastructure, national resources, and partnerships with industry so that students are not stuck. And the talent flow is a real concern. If every strong PhD student leaves in year two, the long-term pipeline suffers. But I'd say the opportunity has never been bigger. The demand for people who truly understand the full stack, from the model down to the kernel, is enormous, and universities are still the best place to learn that deeply.

So my advice is: don't try to be a smaller version of a frontier lab. Be the place that asks the questions they are too busy to ask.

astra-6.text:
I think the resource gap is real, and it does affect what kinds of questions we can tackle. If the goal is to train the largest model, then a university group is probably not in the best position to compete. But I don’t think that has to be the goal of university ML systems research.

One opportunity is to ask how we can make these capabilities accessible with fewer resources. Can we run models more efficiently? Can we adapt them to different hardware or deploy them under tighter memory constraints? Those are systems questions where a good idea can matter more than the size of your compute cluster.

We also have the freedom to explore ideas that may not fit the immediate priorities of a frontier lab. You can rethink an abstraction, investigate a different approach, and build a prototype that helps people see what might be possible. You still need to validate it carefully, especially if you’re making claims about scale, but you don’t necessarily need to reproduce an entire frontier training run to make a useful contribution.

And I think open source is a very important bridge. A university team can develop an idea, make it available, and collaborate with a broader community to test and improve it. So I would frame the opportunity around choosing questions where we have a distinctive contribution, rather than trying to do the same thing as a large lab with a smaller budget.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the resource gap is real, but it also makes the choice of research questions more important. If the goal is to reproduce the largest training run at a frontier lab, that’s very difficult for a university. But ML systems research has many opportunities beyond that.

One direction is to ask how we can make these capabilities accessible under different constraints. Can we run models efficiently on a laptop or a phone? Can we reduce the memory requirement, or support hardware that isn’t the most expensive GPU? Those constraints can lead to interesting systems ideas, and you don’t necessarily need a huge cluster to explore them.

Another opportunity is to build abstractions and open-source infrastructure that help many people innovate. A university group can develop an idea, demonstrate it at a scale where the underlying problem is visible, and enable a broader community to build on it. The impact can be much larger than the resources of the original group.

So I wouldn’t frame the university’s role as competing with a frontier lab on the same benchmark with the same approach. We should choose problems where a new idea matters more than the size of the compute budget, while being honest about what our experiments can establish.
